habitat: Common cranes, also known as Eurasian cranes, have one of the widest distributions of any crane species, breeding from northern Europe across Siberia to eastern Russia and wintering in southern Europe, North Africa, the Middle East, and South Asia. During breeding, they favor boreal forests, wetlands, bogs, and secluded marshes. In winter, they congregate in large numbers on shallow lakes, flooded agricultural fields, grasslands, and mudflats. Key wintering sites include the Hula Valley (Israel), the Duero Basin (Spain), and Khichan (India).
diet: Common cranes are omnivorous with seasonal dietary shifts. During summer, they feed on insects, earthworms, frogs, snakes, small mammals, and bird eggs. In winter, their diet leans heavily toward plant material — grains, seeds, tubers, roots, acorns, and agricultural waste such as rice, maize, and wheat stubble. They are ground-foragers, probing soil with their long, sharp bills. In agricultural areas, they provide ecosystem services by consuming pest insects, but large flocks can damage crops.
behavior: Common cranes are famous for their spectacular migratory flocks — thousands of birds flying in elegant V-formations, communicating with resonant, trumpeting calls audible from kilometers away. Their courtship dances are among the most elaborate in the bird world, involving synchronized bowing, leaping, wing-flapping, stick-tossing, and running. Pairs mate for life, reinforcing their bond through duet calls and dancing. During migration, they use thermals to soar to great heights, reducing energy expenditure over long distances. Cranes navigate using learned routes passed down through generations.
facts: Common cranes are among the largest flying birds, with a wingspan of 2-2.4 meters and standing 100-130 cm tall. Their trumpeting call is produced by an elongated, coiled trachea that acts like a natural brass instrument. They can fly at altitudes exceeding 10,000 meters while crossing the Himalayas. In Celtic mythology, cranes were associated with wisdom and the god Lugh. Cranes are symbols of longevity and fidelity in East Asian art. Their populations are recovering across Europe after centuries of decline.
naming: Crane names might reflect their elegance, long migration, or trumpeting call. Consider names like Dancer, Trumpet, Voyager, Skye, Zephyr, Grace, Aria, Echo, Siberia, or Majestic.
